name: Mate with king and rook
goal: You can mate a lone king with king and rook: shut it in a box, bring your king up, check when the two kings face each other, and never take its last square unless it is mate.

intro.text: A rook on its own cannot give mate, so your king has to join in. The rook marks out a box the lone king cannot leave, your king walks up to guard the rook, and one step at a time the two of them take squares away until the enemy king is stuck on the edge of the board. The usual way to push it back is to wait until the two kings stand face to face, one square apart, and then check with the rook: the lone king has to step back. Near the end you sometimes need a waiting move, a rook move that keeps the box as it is and hands the turn to your opponent. Watch out for stalemate all the way: if the lone king is not in check and has no square to go to, the game is only a draw.

parts.title: King and rook in the corner
parts.keyIdea: The rook shuts the king into a box, and your king guards the rook so the box can get smaller safely.
parts.text: A position from Wikibooks. You are White. Your king and rook start in the corner, and Black's king stands in the centre of the board. Before the rook can do anything useful, your pieces need to work together.

credit.source: Wikibooks, Chess/The Endgame/King and Rook vs. King

notes.text: 1.Kc2, the king to c2, heads for the centre. Later the rook will need the king close by, both to stay safe and to help give mate.
2.Kd3 comes closer again. From d3 the king guards c4, d4 and e4, squares the rook will want to use soon.

3.Ra4 puts the rook on the fourth rank, the fourth row from your side, where it controls the whole row. Black's king on d5 cannot come down the board past it. On a4 the rook is far from Black's king, so it is safe there.

Black's king stepped to e5, and 4.Rd4 slides the rook right next to it. Your king on d3 guards the rook, so it cannot be taken. Now Black's king is shut in to the right of the d-file and above the fourth rank.
The king went to f5, so 5.Re4 moves the rook to e4, still guarded by your king. The box is smaller now: the f-, g- and h-files, above the fourth rank.

parts.title: When the box cannot get smaller yet
parts.keyIdea: If moving the rook in would let the enemy king take it, walk your own king up to guard that square first.
parts.text: The same Wikibooks example, a few moves later. You are White. The rook on e6 keeps Black's king in the top two rows, on the f-, g- and h-files. The rook would like to go to f6, but Black's king on g7 would simply take it there.

credit.source: Wikibooks, Chess/The Endgame/King and Rook vs. King

notes.text: 10.Ke5 brings your king next to the rook. From e5 it guards e6, so the rook is safe if Black's king comes to f7 to attack it.
Black's king did attack the rook from f7, but your king defends it. 11.Kf5 steps up again: from f5 the king guards both e6 and f6.
Black's king went back to g7. With your king on f5 to guard it, 12.Rf6 moves the rook up to f6, and Black's king is left with the g- and h-files on the top two rows.

Black's king went to h7, and 13.Rg6 moves the rook in again, guarded by your king on f5. The only square left for Black's king is h8: it is stuck on the edge, and the mate is close. It still has that square, so this is not stalemate.

parts.title: A king on the edge
parts.keyIdea: When the lone king has one square left, a rook move that is not a check can hand over the turn and force it onto that square.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's king is on the edge, on e8, and your rook on d5 keeps it off the d-file. There is no mate this move. Look at where Black's king could go if it were Black's turn.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: 90.Rd6 is a waiting move. The rook stays on the d-file, so nothing changes for Black's king, but now Black has to move, and the only square left is f8, facing your king on f6. Any rook move along the d-file that stays out of the king's reach would do the same job.
91.Rd8# checks along the back rank, the row Black's king started on, and your king on f6 guards e7, f7 and g7. Black's king has nowhere to go: checkmate.

parts.title: Mate, not stalemate
parts.keyIdea: Before each move against a lone king, make sure it will still have a square to go to, unless your move is checkmate.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's king is shut in on the h-file, and your king on f7 keeps it off the g-file. You can mate in two moves, but there is a trap on the way: on the last move, the move that looks strongest takes away Black's last square without giving check.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: 97.Rg6 puts the rook right next to Black's king, on a square your king guards, and takes h6 away. Black's king has one square left, h8, so it is not stalemate. The rook could go to a6, b6, c6, d6 or e6 just as well.

98.Rh6# checks down the h-file. Your king covers g7 and g8 and the rook covers h7, so Black's king cannot move: checkmate. In the game White played 98.Rg7 instead. The rook on g7, guarded by your king, covered g8 and h7, but it gave no check. Black's king had no legal move and was not in check, so it was stalemate, and the game was drawn.

parts.title: Check when the kings face each other
parts.keyIdea: When the two kings stand opposite each other, one square apart, a rook check drives the lone king back one row.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Your rook on a5 keeps Black's king off the fifth rank, and the two kings stand face to face on the e-file, one square apart. This is the moment to push the king back towards the edge.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: 80.Ra6+ checks along the sixth rank. Black's king cannot come forward, because your king on e4 covers d5, e5 and f5, so it has to go back to the seventh rank.

Black's king stepped to f7, away from yours. 81.Ke5 walks your king up behind the rook, which stays on the sixth rank and keeps the box shut. If Black's king steps in front of yours again, the rook checks again.
Black's king came back to e7, face to face with yours, so 82.Ra7+ drives it to the back rank. Your king on e5 covers d6, e6 and f6, so it cannot come forward.

The king went to f8. 83.Ke6 does not face it yet: it stands a knight's jump away, and now Black has to move. If Black's king steps to e8, in front of yours, the next check is mate. If it goes to g8 instead, your king follows it along the sixth rank until the kings face each other again.

Black's king stepped in front of yours, and 84.Ra8# is mate: the rook checks along the back rank, and your king on e6 covers d7, e7 and f7. That is the usual finish: the kings face each other, and the rook gives check on the edge.
